topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Understanding elementary shapes and angles
topic.scope: measuring angles, types of angles, perpendicular lines, classifying triangles and quadrilaterals, 3D shapes

misconceptions.statement: The angle measure is always the larger number on the protractor scale.
misconceptions.why: Students often ignore the orientation of the angle and just pick the bigger value.
misconceptions.fix: Check which arm of the angle points to zero on the scale and read from that zero.

probe.question: Measure an acute angle pointing to the left.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: A right angle must have one horizontal and one vertical line.
misconceptions.why: Students rely on prototypical orientations of shapes.
misconceptions.fix: A right angle is formed by any two lines meeting at 90 degrees, regardless of rotation.

probe.question: Is this tilted L-shape a right angle?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you see is the only reality

misconceptions.statement: An equilateral triangle must be pointing upwards to be equilateral.
misconceptions.why: Students associate the term with a specific visual image.
misconceptions.fix: A triangle is equilateral if all three sides are equal, regardless of its orientation.

probe.question: Is an upside-down triangle with equal sides equilateral?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: A square is not a rectangle.
misconceptions.why: Students view categories as mutually exclusive rather than hierarchical.
misconceptions.fix: A rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles; a square is a special type of rectangle with equal sides.

misconceptions.statement: To measure an angle, the protractor's centre can be placed anywhere along one arm.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on lining up the baseline and ignore that the centre mark must sit exactly on the vertex.
misconceptions.fix: Place the centre of the protractor exactly on the vertex and the zero line along one arm. Only then does the scale give the right measure.

probe.question: A student puts the protractor's baseline along one arm but the centre mark is a little away from the vertex. Will the reading be correct?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the reading is still correct because the baseline is on the arm.

misconceptions.root_belief: Alignment of any one part of the tool is enough

misconceptions.statement: A longer arm makes the angle bigger.
misconceptions.why: Students judge the size of an angle by how long the drawn arms are, not by the opening between them.
misconceptions.fix: The size of an angle is the amount of turn between its arms. Arms are rays and can be extended without changing the angle.

probe.question: Angle A has arms 3 cm long and angle B has arms 6 cm long, and both open the same amount. Which angle is greater?
probe.wrong_answer: Angle B is greater because its arms are longer.

misconceptions.root_belief: Angle size depends on drawn arm length
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's concept of angle

misconceptions.statement: An angle of exactly 180 degrees is not an angle because it looks like a straight line.
misconceptions.why: Students think an angle must have a visible bend or corner at the vertex.
misconceptions.fix: An angle of 180° is called a straight angle. Its arms point in opposite directions and form a straight line.

probe.question: What is the name of the angle made by a straight line at a point on it, and what is its measure?
probe.wrong_answer: It is not an angle at all, it is just a line.

misconceptions.root_belief: Angles must look bent like corners

misconceptions.statement: A reflex angle is any angle that looks bigger than a right angle.
misconceptions.why: Students use the word reflex loosely for any large-looking angle, without the 180° boundary.
misconceptions.fix: A reflex angle is more than 180° but less than 360°. An angle between 90° and 180° is obtuse.

probe.question: What type of angle is 120°?
probe.wrong_answer: Reflex angle, because it is bigger than a right angle.

misconceptions.root_belief: Angle names have loose size boundaries

misconceptions.statement: Two lines are perpendicular only if they meet at a point and one is drawn upright on the other.
misconceptions.why: Students link perpendicular to a standing vertical on a base and miss that the lines only need to meet at 90°.
misconceptions.fix: Two lines or segments are perpendicular if they intersect at a right angle, in any orientation. The 90° meeting matters, not the direction.

probe.question: Two lines cross at 90° but both are tilted at 45° on the page. Are they perpendicular?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because neither line is standing straight up.

misconceptions.source_hint: research on prototype images in geometry

misconceptions.statement: A triangle with two equal sides cannot be called isosceles if its third side is also nearly equal.
misconceptions.why: Students think the categories need clearly different looks and often confuse triangle names with how close sides appear.
misconceptions.fix: An isosceles triangle has at least two equal sides. Triangle names depend on side lengths, and angle types are a different way to classify.

probe.question: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm. Is it isosceles?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because 6 cm is too close to 5 cm, so it is scalene.

misconceptions.root_belief: Appearance decides the category, not measures

misconceptions.statement: A quadrilateral with all four sides equal must be a square.
misconceptions.why: Students take the equal-sides property alone as the defining feature of a square, ignoring the angles.
misconceptions.fix: A square has four equal sides and four right angles. A figure with four equal sides but no right angles is a rhombus.

probe.question: A four-sided figure has all sides 4 cm but its angles are 60°, 120°, 60° and 120°. What is it?
probe.wrong_answer: A square, because all sides are equal.

misconceptions.root_belief: One shared property defines a shape
misconceptions.source_hint: research on shape classification by van Hiele levels

misconceptions.statement: The edges of a 3D solid are all the lines you can see drawn on its picture, including the curved parts.
misconceptions.why: Students count any visible line or curve as an edge without checking whether two flat faces meet there.
misconceptions.fix: An edge is a line segment where two faces meet. A cylinder or cone has curved surfaces and its circular boundaries are edges, but a curved surface is not an edge.

probe.question: How many faces does a cube have, and how many edges?
probe.wrong_answer: 6 faces and 8 edges, counting the corners as edges.

misconceptions.root_belief: Edges, faces and vertices are used interchangeably
